title: Here Is What It Takes to Make Effective Education Technology
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer argues that effective education technology requires technologists to understand how learning actually happens in schools and educators to understand how software gets made. Neither side needs to become expert in the other's field, but they need enough empathy to build products that multiply rather than merely add their skills. His central illustration is a 44-second video of a teacher making roughly a dozen instructional decisions while handling one student's work and noticing another's head down. Meyer uses it to show that the teacher-student interaction precedes and determines subject learning, so a product that treats learning as writing to a database misses most of what matters. Students are also constantly learning about the world, adults, power and themselves, not only the subject matter. The piece is brief and written from inside a curriculum-software company, but its claim about the complexity of classroom teaching is clear and well grounded.
points: Technologists often model learning on their own laptop-based experience (Stack Overflow, YouTube, chatbots), which has little in common with learning in a classroom.
Ed tech teams get better products when technologists learn that learning is contingent on teacher skill, classroom social environment and the school calendar.
Educators on those teams benefit from learning that platform constraints are liberating, because they let users start using a tool rather than learning it.
The 44-second classroom clip shows a teacher making around a dozen decisions at once, which illustrates how much expertise any teaching tool must work within.
The way a teacher conducts the interaction (inquisitive or presumptuous, empathetic or punitive) is highly predictive of how much math a student learns.
quotes: Neither group will become an expert in the other’s domain. But once they cross a certain threshold of empathy and understanding, they can start to make truly wild stuff together.

The technologists who once assumed learning is something like performing write operations on a database now understand that those write operations are contingent on circumstances like teacher skill, the social environment of the classroom, the school calendar, etc.

Technologists need to understand that the experiences they have learning in front of their laptops during their workdays—typing questions into Stack Overflow; watching explanatory YouTube videos; perhaps even riffing with some AI chatbot—while powerful and legitimate have very little in common with the work of learning in schools.
That interaction between the teacher and student both precedes and determines any learning about the day’s subject! Their interaction isn’t about math per se.

Students are learning constantly in classrooms. It’s just that what they’re learning isn’t always explicitly about the subject matter. They’re learning about the world, about grownups, about power, and about themselves.

When education technologists appreciate and learn to work within the complexity of classroom teaching, when educators and technologists enlist one another in partnership, well, okay, the odds are still very long but I like them a lot better.
